job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in the flat above their noodle restaurant, Golden Bowl, on Harbour Street, so I wake up to the smell of broth. I'm in the kitchen by eleven for the lunch rush, chopping or on the till, then I'm at my laptop between two and five. I use AI for everything, from drafting emails to debugging my robot arm code. I finished a mechatronics degree, which is electrical and mechanical engineering with robotics, eight months ago, top of my year. My final project was a robot arm that portions rice and noodles, and I interned at a packaging-machine maker and an industrial automation firm. I've had no offer yet, but I've been busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a reality check. Hype cycles are normal, and the people who build real things do fine afterwards. I'd tell friends to ignore the headlines and make something people pay for. I'd post about it, probably with a video of my robot arm making a rice bowl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a slow market, a slow graduate scheme season and a lot of people waiting. I've sent 75 applications and had five interviews. I have about two months of savings, a loan of about ten thousand, and my parents covering rent. I earn a bit on the side in the restaurant, which keeps me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, but I'd also pitch my portioning robot to three other restaurants on Harbour Street, as a rental. I'd charge a monthly fee and see if I can make 600 a month by summer. I'd keep the interviews going with the automation firms because they'll pay me to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Itchy. I don't like waiting, and I like it even less when I've got an idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would restaurants rent a robot arm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Labour costs are brutal. My parents pay four staff, and rent, and the margins are thin. If an arm saves them two shifts a week, it pays for itself. Restaurant owners are practical, and they'll pay for what saves them money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents think of your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum worries I'm wasting my degree on noodles. Dad is quietly proud and let me test the arm in the kitchen. I'd say they'd back me if the numbers worked, because they respect money earned the hard way.

say: I'd say it's a **reality check**, and people who build real things do fine afterwards.
I'd post a **video** of my robot arm making a rice bowl.
think: It's a slow market with a lot of people waiting, and I have two months of **savings** and a loan.
My idea has a **real customer** next door: restaurants with thin margins.

Aim for **600 a month** in rentals by summer.
Keep interviewing at **automation firms** that would pay me to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good kind of disruption, because it rewards people who build and punishes people who wait for permission. I'd tell friends to stop complaining and start learning. I'd also say governments should stay out of the way and cut red tape for small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For junior coders, it's rough, since the entry-level work gets done by a tool. For a mechatronics engineer, it's an advantage, because I can build what the software controls. Small businesses will want automation they can run without a team, and I can sell that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my arm into a small product, with an AI that handles orders and stock. I'd sign up three paying restaurants and take a part-time job at an automation firm to learn the commercial side. I'd also put my savings into a better camera and a second arm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up. I'd be nervous about money, but I like where it's heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said governments should cut red tape. Which red tape?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Food safety paperwork for a machine that touches meals, licensing and the cost of insurance. It's important to get it right, but for a small firm the forms alone can take a month. A clear one-page route for small automation would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who's worried about their job being automated by your product?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not hiding it. In a small restaurant, the arm covers a task and the cook is freed for the hard part, but I'd be honest that shifts may shrink. I'd want to help the owner keep their staff by growing the business, not cutting.

say: I'd say this rewards people who **build** and punishes people who wait for permission.
I'd say governments should stay out of the way and cut **red tape** for small firms.

Sign up **three paying restaurants** and take a part-time automation job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a rocket launch. I'd say don't wait for the government, build now. I'd say families and small firms need to team up, because big institutions will be slow. I'd tell friends to learn how to run a business, since wages won't be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a lot of jobs, including mine as a junior engineer, disappear in two years. But the robot side runs about three years behind, so hands-on machinery stays in demand until about 2031. If I own machines and customers, I'm on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the restaurant robots. I'd borrow some money from Dad against the restaurant's savings and build four more arms. I'd pitch every restaurant, café and canteen within an hour's drive. And I'd keep a steady part-time job at an automation firm, in case it doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Racing heart, big grin, a little nausea. Like the top of a roller coaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said borrow from your dad. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say what's the plan, and I'd show him a spreadsheet. He'd say if it fails we lose the savings, and I'd say I know. He'd probably say yes, because he took a risk opening Golden Bowl with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a salaried job in automation and work my way back. A failure in two years of AGI doesn't ruin me. The worse failure is sitting still and having nothing to show.

I'd tell friends to learn to **run a business**, since wages won't be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a good runway. I'd say go build, and tell friends to pick the one skill that's hardest to copy. I'd say families should talk about money earlier, not later, because plans change faster than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, because I'd be early on the robots. I'd have a couple of years of customers, a name and a cash flow by the time AI does thinking at full strength. And the real robots arrive about 2034, and I'd be buying them for my business, not competing with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the arm business within the first year, hire a student by year two and licence the software to other restaurants by year three. I'd also put money into an index fund each month and not touch it. And I'd keep Dad's restaurant as the demonstration site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Maybe too excited. My mum tells me to calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your first real profit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off my loan, honestly, then give Dad a share for his help. I'd also buy Mum a new rice cooker, because the old one is held together with tape. It's small, but it'd mean something to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could trip you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overconfidence, probably. I move fast and sometimes ignore details. I'd hire someone careful, maybe a food-safety consultant, to keep me honest. Fast and careful is the combination I'd need.

I'd tell families to talk about **money** earlier, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time to prepare, and I'd say don't waste it on waiting. I'd say let the market do its work and let people start businesses. I'd tell friends to get qualified and own something small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well. In ten years I'd have a real business, maybe a few restaurants using my arms, or a job as a senior engineer if the business didn't take off. And I'd have built savings. The danger is the first year, when money is thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business next year, keep my loan on schedule, and move out in two years into a small flat of my own. I'd probably get a master's in robotics in parallel, part time. And I'd help my brother's friends learn practical skills, because I like teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, to be honest. Maybe a bit smug, but I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different if you were wrong about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be the guy who spent a year building robot arms nobody wanted, and I'd still have the skills. I'd get a salaried job and nobody would hold it against me. That's why I can take risks, as I have a family safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about people who can't take risks like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to have an easier route in: apprenticeships, small business loans, mentors. I came up with Dad's restaurant behind me, and I know a lot of people don't have that. I'd mentor some myself.

I'd tell friends to get **qualified** and own something small.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, even though it's the one I'm best placed to ride. It'd leave the people without a family business or savings with nothing. What would help is simple small-business rules, apprenticeships and loans that don't need a rich family behind you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as fearless as I sound. I'm lucky to have a family restaurant behind me. I'd like to use that luck on something that helps other people too.

headlineQuote: I'm not as fearless as I sound. I'm lucky to have a family restaurant behind me.
portrait: Ben is a 23-year-old **mechatronics** graduate, top of his year, living above his parents' noodle restaurant, Golden Bowl.
He has had 75 applications and five interviews, with two months of savings and a **ten thousand** loan.
He is traditional and free-market, wants less **red tape** for small firms, and uses AI daily and is early with new technology.
He is turning a robot arm that portions rice and noodles into a **rental business** and sees ownership as the safe position.
He admits his **family safety net** lets him take risks and wants apprenticeships and small loans for others.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries him most, mainly for people without a family business or savings.
whatWouldHelp: He wants simple small-business rules, **apprenticeships** and loans that don't need a rich family behind you.
